tools.what_it_times: send to receive of its own monitoring messages, end to end through the cluster: the produce service stamps each record with its wall clock and the consume service subtracts its own. SingleClusterMonitor runs both services in one JVM, so one wall clock; the service factories let a producer and a consumer run as separate processes or hosts, and the README describes pointing the two services at two clusters joined by MirrorMaker. Separately, a produce delay from send to acknowledgment is timed inside the producer

clock_and_resolution.finding: Wall clock at millisecond resolution on both sides: System.currentTimeMillis() in the produce service, written into the record's JSON as its time field, and System.currentTimeMillis() in the consume service, which subtracts it. Neither side reads a monotonic clock, and nothing corrects for an offset between two processes' or hosts' clocks.

odd_values.finding: The difference is recorded with no test of its sign into a Kafka metrics sensor carrying an average, a maximum and percentiles. The average keeps a negative value. The percentiles do not: kafka-clients' Percentiles is built with a floor of 0.0 and pins any value below it to that floor, logging it only at debug level, so a negative latency enters the 99th, 99.9th and 99.99th percentiles as 0 ms, uncounted. The tool's own comment says two extra buckets catch values below 0 and above the maximum; kafka-clients 2.8.2 has no such buckets. The only latency counter counts records later than the SLA.

warnings.finding: none found. The README describes the end-to-end latency metrics and the two-cluster arrangement without any word on clocks, synchronisation or negative values.

tools.what_it_times: send to receive of its canary messages, end to end through the cluster, in one process with two Kafka clients: the producer stamps the message and a consumer goroutine subtracts. Both readings are one wall clock

clock_and_resolution.finding: Wall clock cut to whole milliseconds on both sides: time.Now().UnixNano() / 1000000, which reads Go's wall clock and not its monotonic one, written into the message as its timestamp field and subtracted by the consumer from its own reading.

odd_values.finding: Recorded with no test of its sign into a Prometheus histogram whose lowest bucket is 5 ms by default, so a negative value is counted in the same bucket as a fast message and shows only as a lower sum. The log line at verbosity 1 prints each duration, sign included, but the tool the repository ships to read those lines, tools/canary_latencies.py, matches durations with the pattern [0-9]+, which cannot match a minus sign, so it skips every negative duration, uncounted.

warnings.finding: none found. The README documents the latency histograms and their buckets in milliseconds and says nothing about clocks or negative values.

tools.what_it_times: four things, by workload. ProduceBench times send to acknowledgment inside the producer. ConsumeBench times the wait between consecutive non-empty polls of one consumer, charged to every record of the batch, which is not a message's trip. ConsumeBench's timestamp record processor times end to end: ProduceBench's payload generator writes its wall clock into each record and the consumer, another agent and possibly another host, subtracts its own. RoundTripWorkload reports no latency at all

clock_and_resolution.finding: Every reading is Time.SYSTEM.milliseconds(), System.currentTimeMillis(): the wall clock in whole milliseconds, so the end-to-end figure crosses two agents' clocks.

odd_values.finding: Two dispositions. The timestamp record processor clamps: histogram.add(Long.max(0L, (latency - histogramMinMs) / histogramStepMs)) puts every negative end-to-end latency in the lowest bucket, reported as histogramMinMs, uncounted. Trogdor's Histogram itself refuses a negative with an exception, 'invalid negative value.': in ProduceBench the exception is thrown inside the send callback and only logged by the producer, so the sample is lost; in ConsumeBench it aborts the task.

warnings.finding: none found. trogdor/README.md describes the latency each workload measures without any word on clocks.

tools.what_it_times: per window, not per event: the processing job's wall clock at a window's last write to Redis minus the window's start, which comes from the event time the generator wrote. In the intended cluster nine of ten generators run on hosts other than the processor's, so the difference crosses machines' clocks

clock_and_resolution.finding: Wall clocks in milliseconds: the generator's System/currentTimeMillis read once at start, from which each event's scheduled time is computed, and the processor's System.currentTimeMillis() at each one-second flush. The window is ten seconds, so the reported figure includes it.

odd_values.finding: The tool writes every difference to updated.txt with no test of its sign. The analysis notebook the repository ships keeps only values at or above the window length before subtracting it, so a window whose latency comes out negative is dropped, uncounted, and a second cell drops values of a second or less.

warnings.finding: none found; the README describes updated.txt as the latency from the last event to the Redis write, which the code does not compute.
